This petition has been filed in public interest under Article 32 of the Constitution in the wake of serious violations and abuse of children who are forcefully detained in circuses, in many instances, without any access to their families under extreme inhuman conditions.

The Petitioner filed this petition following a series of incidents where the Petitioner came in contact with many children who were trafficked into performing in circuses. The activities that are undertaken in these circuses deprive the children of their basic fundamental rights. Most of them are trafficked from some poverty-stricken areas of Nepal as well as from backward districts of India. After detailed research and enquiry, the Petitioner found that organized crime of trafficking of children for Indian circuses, particularly from Nepal is rampant. Mostly, these children are sold to the circus owners either by the agents or their relatives or sometimes the poor parents are lured into the web by promising high salaries, luxurious life, etc. Children are frequently physically, emotionally and sexually abused in these places. There is violation of the Juvenile Justice Act and all International treaties and Conventions related to Human Rights and Child Rights where India is a signatory.

The employment of children in circus involves violation of several Fundamental and Statutory Rights, namely, right to education; right to freedom of expression; competency to enter into contract for working in circus; existing labour laws and legitimacy of contracts; and all statutory provisions dealing with child labour.

Solicitor General appearing for the Union of India broadened the scope of this petition and submitted a detailed report dealing with the problem of trafficking in children.

The Supreme Court discussed the issue of trafficking, factors that cause trafficking, available legislations, India’s obligations under International and Regional Instruments, National Plans and Policies to combat human trafficking, and existing child protection mechanisms.

The court issued the following directions to the Central Government regarding children working in the Indian circuses:

(i) Issue suitable notifications prohibiting the employment of children in circuses within two months from the date of the order in order to implement the fundamental right of the children under Article 21A of the Constitution of India.

(ii) Conduct simultaneous raids in all the circuses to liberate the children and check the violation of fundamental rights of the children. The rescued children be kept in the Care and Protective Homes till they attain the age of 18 years.

(iii) Talk to the parents of the children and in case they are willing to take their children back to their homes, they may be directed to do so after proper verification.

(iv) Frame proper scheme of rehabilitation of rescued children from circuses.

The defendant is accused of promoting and facilitating the international departure of two women for sexual exploitation in Spain and of practicing the tentative crime of international trafficking of people for sexual exploitation women (article 231, caput of the Penal Code). In the 1st Instance Court, the defendant was convicted to 3 years and 9 months of imprisonment, converted to 2 penalties restrictive of rights, for two tentative crimes of international trafficking of people for sexual exploitation (article 231, caput of the Penal Code).

The defendant appealed to the 2nd Instance Court, alleging that the crime had prescribed and that the accusation of the practice of the tentative crime of international trafficking of people for sexual exploitation (article 231, caput of the Penal Code) was not a valid accusation since the departure from the national territory was not consumed due to the police intervention upon boarding the victims and that the victims knew that they would travel abroad to practice prostitution.

The 2nd Instance Court denied the appeal, affirming that the crime of international trafficking of people for sexual exploitation (article 231, caput of the Penal Code) did not prescribe, that it is not necessary to have completed all the acts of the crime to characterize the tentative of its commitment and that the crime is characterized when all the measures needed to facilitate and promote the victim`s departure from the country are taken, even if the victims knew that they would travel abroad to practice prostitution.

(In relation to B.’s testimony, the Århus District Court held on 22 May 2008 that the defendants were not entitled to be informed about or attend the hearing in question, a decision that was upheld by the Western High Court on 6 June 2008; see Western High Court judgment, V2008.S-1142-08 – TfK2008.669). When victim A. filed the police report in March 2008 – through the aid of a Slovak interpreter as she did not speak Danish – she identified the house of the defendants as the place where she had resided for purposes of prostitution. As per A.’s request, she received assistance in returning to Slovakia after filing the police report in order to give birth to her baby there. The defendant, upon a prior understanding with an unidentified person, recruited a young woman by deceiving her and abusing the position of vulnerability of the victim who had a poor financial situation in view of transporting her to Cyprus, for purposes of sexual exploitation. Date of arrest: Information is not available.

The first defendant was a managing director of a travel company, of which the second defendant was its international affairs manager. Thus, on several occasions, the first and the second defendants, together or separately, brought two or three victims at a time to travel a roundtrip from Thailand to Malaysia, Singapore (in one case, to Vietnam instead of Malaysia and Singapore), Germany, Switzerland or Italy, and return to Malaysia with a transit in Japan. While waiting for the transit in Japan, the 1st and 2nd defendants would plan for all of them to pretend to miss the connecting flights and ask the Japanese immigration for a temporary entry into Japan while waiting for a new connecting flight. Once they were granting temporary permission to enter Japan, the 1st defendant sold the victims to several disguised brothels in Japan. One of brothel owners identified by many victims was Ms Kasumi, a Taiwanese national living in Japan. The defendant with his accomplices recruited and transported a woman to Istanbul, Turkey by deceiving her, abusing the position of vulnerability of the victim, who has a poor financial situation, for purposes of sexual exploitation.

Ms Emerson forced three young women, two of whom were underage at the time of the offence, into prostitution. The victims were confined inside a Gatineau area condominium furnished only with a mattress and forced to prostitute. The victims were also transported to hotels and homes to service clients. In March/April 2004, defendant O.M.A., in cooperation with co-defendants E.K.I., B.K.I. and L.L.I., fraudulently promised their victim a job in Germany. During an investigation into massage parlours in the Buffalo, New York area, law enforcement picked up a woman whom they thought was a victim outside the Hong Kong Acupressure in Amherst, New York. The underage victims, who were descendants of an indigenous community in Ecuador, were arrested by the police for selling products in an unauthorized place. The defendants were charged with the offence of human trafficking.

The defendant works at a recruitment agency as a field officer and has been involved in recruiting Indonesians to work in the Middle East and other countries. It was discovered by the police that H.Subroto and his team were not licensed to carry on a recruitment company for foreign workers, instead they were known to transport women to foreign countries through illegal means.

The plaintiffs were former child camel jockeys and their parents. Ultimately, the federal District Court for the Eastern District of Kentucky dismissed this case for lack of personal jurisdiction over the named defendant.

Patama Kampha, the third defendant, was the daughter of the first and the second defendants. She went to work in Japan and married a Japanese man. Ms Yenny Carolina Roa Calvo and S.M.O.G. met at a nightclub in Pereira in late 2006. The defendant put S.M.O.G. in contact with Mr Héctor Fernando Gutiérrez, a 38-year-old Colombian citizen. Mr Gutierrez took photos of S.M.O.G. and mailed them to a contact in Panama. He helped the victim fill in the documents necessary to receive her passport and took her to a travel agent to claim the plane ticket that had been sent from Panama. Mr Gutierrez later accompanied S.M.O.G. to a finance agency, where she withdrew money that would be used for her personal needs and for the travel expenses. He finally took her to the airport and instructed her on how to behave during the trip. He also described to her the people who would meet her in Panama.

The victim was picked up in Panama by members of a criminal organization and was then confined to the Crystal Moon nightclub, where she was forced to work as a prostitute. She was required to pay back a range of expenses as well as a high rate of interest that was added to this debt. Expenses included money spent on flights, the rental of dresses that she had to use to attract customers, the rental of the lock she used to store her belongings, phone calls, housing, food and transport.

In the case of Sieders and Yotchomchin several young Thai women were put to work as sex workers in Sydney brothels operated by the accused to repay an artificial debt of AUD 45,000 per person. Ms Yotchomchin, an Australian resident of Thai background, owned and managed one brothel in Strathfield and two in Parramatta. Mr Sieders and his Thai wife owned and operated one brothel in Penrith [Sieders v R; Somsri v R (2008) 72 NSWLR 417, 421-422]. The victims were instructed that their debt reflected the costs of their flights, visas, and the ‘service’ of being brought to Australia [R v Johan Sieders and Somsri Yotchomchin [2006] NSWDC 184, [17]]. The victims were not free to cease work nor leave the defendants’ employment and would not receive any payment until their debts had been repaid [R v Johan Sieders and Somsri Yotchomchin [2006] NSWDC 184, [37]]. The indictment specified the period of offending as December 1, 2003 to May 31, 2004, when the defendants’ brothels were searched by law enforcement and immigration officials (Operation Turqoise) [R v Johan Sieders and Somsri Yotchomchin [2006] NSWDC 184, [6]-[7]; Sieders v R; Somsri v R (2008) 72 NSWLR 417, 422]. The case came to the attention of Australian authorities after one of the victims had begged one of her clients to contact the authorities to help her escape [R v Johan Sieders and Somsri Yotchomchin [2006] NSWDC 184, [51]].

During the trial, five women, all Thai nationals, were called on by the Crown to give evidence about the sexual servitude they experienced in the defendants’ brothels. Prior to the commencement of the trial a suppression order was imposed due to the sensitive nature of the women’s testimony[ R v Johan Sieders and Somsri Yotchomchin [2006] NSWDC 184, [8]], and the victims were subsequently referred to by the pseudonyms AA, LK, WS, PN, and WP. LK, WS, PN, and WP worked at the premises during the period specified in the indictment while Ms AA had performed a sufficient number of sexual services to discharge her debt prior to this time [Sieders v R; Somsri v R (2008) 72 NSWLR 417, 421]. Justice Campbell calculated that the evidence indicated that this would have required AA to provide some 900 to 1000 sexual services of thirty minutes duration [Sieders v R; Somsri v R (2008) 72 NSWLR 417, 423]. The trafficking process and the conditions under which the women were kept were evinced through the women's testimonies, which are discussed individually below [R v Johan Sieders and Somsri Yotchomchin [2006] NSWDC 184, [18]].
The Trafficking Process
The five women were trafficked into sexual servitude through a lengthy process which involved several parties seeking to make profit. The available evidence suggests that all five women, when in Thailand, came into contact with Ms Montha Phuncharaen, referred to as Pat by the victims, a Thai woman responsible for coordinating arrangements in Thailand including the initial recruitment of women for trafficking [R v Johan Sieders and Somsri Yotchomchin [2006] NSWDC 184, [18]]. It was Ms Phuncharaen who obtained the victims’ agreement to engage in sex work in Australia on the basis that they would work in brothels to repay an artificial ‘contractual’ debt of AUD 45,000 [Sieders v R; Somsri v R (2008) 72 NSWLR 417, 421, 437]. Some of the women were told of this amount from the beginning; others were deceived and agreed on the basis of a significantly lower amount [R v Johan Sieders and Somsri Yotchomchin [2006] NSWDC 184, [60]]. Ms LK, for instance, testified that she was not informed of the amount at any time prior to leaving Thailand [Sieders v R; Somsri v R (2008) 72 NSWLR 417, 421].

None of the women were informed of the exploitative and restrictive working and living conditions they would be subjected to while repaying their debts. Several women gave evidence that after agreeing to the contract, Ms Phuncharaen threatened to harm them and their families should they not work hard enough to repay the debt. It was later revealed that Ms Phuncharaen received substantial compensation for delivering each victim to the defendants in Australia [Sieders v R; Somsri v R (2008) 72 NSWLR 417, 422, 436-437.].

The entry into Australia was facilitated by Ms Phuncharaen by organising tourist visas for each victim. Each of the victims were escorted by a male minder on the flights to Sydney who handed them directly to one of the defendants or, on occasions, to Mr Sieders’ wife, Ms Rapeparn Arpornrat. To disguise the women as tourists, each had a small sum of money and a return airline ticket placed in her possession for the duration of the trip. Upon arrival in Australia, either Mr Sieders or Ms Yotchomchin immediately confiscated all funds, the victims’ passports, and their return airline tickets [Sieders v R; Somsri v R (2008) 72 NSWLR 417, 421-422].

After receiving the victims, the defendants then liaised with a corrupt immigration official, Mr Mofazzal Haque Kazi, to fraudulently obtain bridging refugee visas for the women [R v Johan Sieders and Somsri Yotchomchin [2006] NSWDC 184, [21]]. In some cases, the debt owed was increased to account for this process [Sieders v R; Somsri v R (2008) 72 NSWLR 417, 422].

The victims were taken directly to the defendants’ brothels, where they were required to begin servicing clients immediately. It was not until this point that the rules and conditions of their employment and debt were fully explained to the victims. The lives of the women were now controlled by Mr Sieders, his wife and Ms Yotchomchin. All arrangements were made without consultation and without the consent of the victims. The defendants determined where the victims worked each day, the hours of work, and they personally transferred the victims between brothels [Sieders v R; Somsri v R (2008) 72 NSWLR 417, 421, 422, 438]. The victims lived in the brothels and worked up to 13 hour a day, 7 days a week [R v Johan Sieders and Somsri Yotchomchin [2006] NSWDC 184, [71]].

If a woman wished to leave the brothel, permission had to be granted by either defendant. Ms LK, for instance, gave evidence that on at least one occasion when she sought to leave the brothel because of sickness, permission was not granted. The women were explicitly told that they ‘could not go anywhere’ until they had discharged their debts, and threatened that if a woman did try to escape then ‘it will be found out where they went’[Sieders v R; Somsri v R (2008) 72 NSWLR 417,438.].

The court proceedings later illustrated the vulnerabilities of the women whilst in Australia, including their inability to work legally whilst on tourist visas, the extremely limited English language skills, and the lack of contacts to persons outside the sex industry, which gave the victims no choice but to comply with their traffickers’ demands and work to pay of their debts [Sieders v R; Somsri v R (2008) 72 NSWLR 417, 439.].

With the exception of the occasional tip by clients, amounting to AUD 20 or less, at no time were the women permitted to retain any funds paid by the clients for themselves. Any money earned had to go directly to the defendants, who would then deduct the amount earned from the debt owed. To that end, Mr Sieders and Ms Yotchomchin maintained a rather elaborate accounting system so that some of the money would be used to reduce the victims’ debt, while some money went straight to the brothels. According to the evidence of Ms AA and Ms WP, the defendants developed an arrangement whereby the women would work at the rate of AUD 55 for fifteen minutes of sexual services, with AUD 35 deducted from the debt, AUD 85 for 30 minutes, with AUD 50 deducted, and AUD 150 for 1 hour of services, with AUD 85 deducted. According to calculations made by Justice Campbell, in order to be free of the AUD 45,000 debt at these rates, each woman would be required to perform 1,286 sets of 15-minute services, or 900 sets of 30-minute services, or 530 sets of 1-hour services before she was permitted to retain any money herself. It took four of the five women months to discharge their debts, often working 7 days a week [Sieders v R; Somsri v R (2008) 72 NSWLR 417, 421-423]. While the women were free to leave once the debt was repaid, many chose to continue working for the defendants.

Ms LK was the only victim who did not repay her debt before the trafficking operation was brought to an end. In an attempt to escape her conditions, LK began asking her Thai speaking clients, and then in broken English to her Australian clients, to help her escape. Eventually a client contacted the Department of Immigration, and search warrants were executed on the Strathfield and Penrith brothels in May 2004. Due to the illegality of the women's work under their visas, several women, including LK, were placed in the Villawood Immigration Detention Centre before being returned to Thailand. Whilst in immigration detention, Mr Sieders’ wife threatened LK that her ‘family will be in trouble and will never live in peace again’, should she disclose any information to the authorities [Sieders v R; Somsri v R (2008) 72 NSWLR 417, 422.; Sieders v R; Somsri v R [2008] NSWCCA 187, [58], [65]].

The defendant recruited and transported in 2004 three women to Ankara, Turkey by deceiving them, under the pretext of finding a job, for purposes of sexual exploitation. All three victims were tortured, physically abused, ill-treated and subjected to inhuman and degrading treatment in order to ensure they provide sexual services against their will.

During the fall of 2006, the defendant forced victim S. to engage in sexual relations for money with witnesses T.E., E.O., N.M. and E.B.O in T.E.’s domicile. The defendant approached customers and provided transportation for them from and to the nightclub. The victim also had to perform sexual acts in the back of a store with several other men. Victim S. initially stated that she had been threatened and coerced into having sexual relations with these men for money by the defendant, but subsequently, recanted her testimony at the judiciary investigative stage, saying that she had done this willingly.

The Mehedinti Tribunal also found that the defendant forced victim B.S. to have sexual relations with several men while at a nightclub, under the pretext that they needed to cover the nightclub tab and the hotel room. Victim B.S. initially testified that she had been threatened and coerced into engaging in sexual relations with those men but she later recanted her testimony.

The Tribunal found that both the victims and other witnesses had recanted their testimonies due to undue pressure from the defendant and the defendant’s family. The Tribunal found evidence of threats from the defendant and his family. In the case of victim B.S., they threatened her and said that they could procure her with a medical certificate that would make her non responsible for her own actions.

The accused solicited clients with erotic advertisements and pictures of the victims published on Internet websites, transported the victims to hotels to engage in sex acts, and took control of all earnings, amounting to an estimated $400,000 over a two year period for one victim, and approximately two months for the other.

Mr. Nakpangi manipulated the girls to believe they were in a romantic relationship with him, and then used threats, intimidation and physical violence to control the girls. When one victim wanted to quit, Nakpangi imposed a $100,000 exit fee on the victim.

Ms B. was 18 at the time of the defendant's arrest, she had been a prostitute since she was 14, and was homeless at the time. When she was 15 the defendant became her pimp. He gave her false identification in the name of Tiffany La Rue, a 20 year old. She turned over a total of $360 to him. She tried to leave his control, though he chased her and assaulted her. He even threatened to kidnap her brother as well.

Ms. S. was 14 and a ward of the Children's Aid Society when she met the accused, it was a chance meeting. She became a prostitute; she gave her earnings to the accused, a total of $65,000. He was fully aware of her age. Mr. Nakpangi acted as the pimp of Ms. S., he facilitated meeting for sex. The fee was $200 for a half hour, $300 for one hour. He transported her, provided cell phone contract.

Mr. Nakpangi was initially arrested for a Highway Offence when he was driving a BMW with illegal identification.

The defendants have recruited several young women, transported them to Germany and promised they will find them jobs. Being in a foreign country and with no means of support, the young women have agreed to have intercourse with different persons appointed by the defendants, who also collected the money from the clients for their benefit. The young women were permanently supervised, some being taken their IDs. Their freedom of movement was restricted and they were subject to different pressures and abuses in order to prostitute.

The Court have seized the following amounts from the defendants:

- EUR 49,100 from A.M.

- EUR 2,000 from R.C.P.

The laws applied were Law no. 678/2001 on preventing and combating human trafficking, the Romanian Criminal Code and the Romanian Criminal Procedure Code.

In April 2002, co-defendants S.M.P and S.F.E. left Romania and rented a “living space” in town E. in Italy. Throughout 2003-2004, the three co-defendants recruited, transported, harboured and transferred several young women -including victims E.N.B., M.S.N. and U.M,- to Italy for the purpose of sexual exploitation. In September 2003, defendant S.M.P. took advantage of the poor financial situation of U.M.’s family, and in the presence of her family, proposed to take U.M. to Italy to find her a job. S.M.P. said he would pay the cost for all the necessary documentation and other expenses. Once in Italy, however, he did not find her the promised job, but rather told her that she should engage in prostitution. U.M. refused and she had to resort to begging in the streets. During this time, she paid the proceeds from her begging to defendant S.F.E.’s concubine. While these facts were established during the investigation, and through U.M.’s testimony, U.M. subsequently retracted her testimony and tried to exonerate the defendants claiming that the initial incriminating testimony was a result of her fear that she would get into trouble with the police if she did not say what they wanted to hear. In October, 2004, defendant S.F.E. took advantage of victim M.S.’ family situation, proposed to take her to Italy where he would find her a job, confirming that he would take care of all costs and that she would not be prostituting herself or begging. After a month in Italy, S.F.E. had still not found her a job and, when M.S. confronted him, he told her that she would have to prostitute herself. She prostituted herself for 45 days and she gave half of the proceeds to S.F.E. Similarly to U.M., M.S. recanted her initial testimony in which she incriminated the defendants. She claimed that upon arriving in Bucharest she was ill (cardiac problems and other health issues) and that this is why she testified that she had been compelled by defendant S.F.E. to prostitute herself.

In the summer of 2004, S.F.E.’s concubine and S.U.’s wife tried to persuade victim E.N.B. to go to Italy where they guaranteed her a job; the victim refused because she feared the prospect of prostitution. Nevertheless, co-defendants S.U. and S.F.E. convinced the victim and her parents to send the victim to Italy. Once she arrived in Italy, defendant S.F.E. told her that he could not find a job for her and that she had to prostitute herself. In order to pay back the defendant, the victim prostituted herself for approximately one month in 2005, after which she was sold to an Albanian panderer. E.N.B. confirmed that victim M.S., along with other girls, had engaged in prostitution.

A police officer caught an undocumented person distributing flyers offering work in a shop that would be opening soon. As a result of this encounter, a general inspection was carried out at the shop on the suspicion that the persons working there were not registered. A young man was working in the ironing shop and identified himself as A.M. He was not authorized to work in Belgium. He was not permitted to stay in Belgium more than three months as he was not registered with the necessary agency. He had arrived from Bulgaria about one month prior to his detection. He was staying in Ghent, at an apartment belonging to the mother of one of the defendants. He later came into contact with another Bulgarian person who offered A.M. work, knowing that A.M. was not authorized to work. A.M. usually worked 48 hours per week. One of the defendants picked him up and dropped him off at the shop for work. He worked from Monday to Saturday, earning EUR 600 per month and paying EUR 250 per month for his lodging and food. A.M. did not think his salary was high enough and wished to return to Bulgaria.

The court established that the victim, H.A.D., came to the city of Sibiu in the month of July of 2006. In the autumn of the same year, she lived for a period in the apartment owned by the defendant. Around December 2006, the victim returned to Sibiu and at that moment the defendant claimed the payment of the phone bill in amount of RON 700 (approximately USD 200) corresponding to the period the victim stayed in his apartment. Since the victim did not dispose of such sum of money, the defendant forced her to practice prostitution with men he would recruit. All the money resulting from such activity was retained by the defendant.

The defendant was caught in the act of charging a sum of money from an undercover investigator for the sexual services of the victim.

The accused was paid to daily transport the complainant to and from the secondary high school that she attended. There were other students who were also so transported. On several occasions in the year 2006 the accused drove the vehicle with the complainant and three (3) other male minors all over the parish. During these occasions the three male minors indecently assaulted the complainant, whilst the accused told her to comply as it would be over soon. The acts were recorded on a cellular telephone by one of the male minors. The male accused pleaded guilty on a subsequent occasion after the matter was put before the court. They were going to give evidence against the accused as per his role in the matter.

The appellant, D., was a single, 26 year old woman who was a citizen of Moldova. She claimed that in 2006 she was offered the opportunity to travel to Israel to work in eldercare. After agreeing to this she was transported through Egypt to Israel with her traffickers intending that she would work as a prostitute. During the journey, which lasted approximately one month, she suffered starvation and harsh weather conditions. A person also attempted to rape her.

On 19 November 2006 D. was caught by the Israeli authorities while trying to cross the Israeli-Egyptian border. The Immigration Administration referred her to a shelter for victims of human trafficking. On 12 December 2006 the respondent granted D. a B-1 permit for humanitarian reasons and for the purpose of assisting the police with their investigation. The permit expired on 30 June 2009 and was later extended to 31 December 2007. On 1 July 2007 D. requested that the respondent grant her a temporary B-1 permit for a year. Her application included a supporting letter from the shelter’s social worker. On 18 September 2007 the respondent rejected the application on the grounds that there was not sufficient evidence to prove that D. was a victim of trafficking. The respondent claimed that the appellant was caught as she tried to enter Israel near the Egyptian border.

On 28 October 2007 the police sent a memo to the director of the shelter that hosted D. The memo stated that the police did not succeed in substantiating the material in its possession in order to have sufficient evidence for trafficking in persons. The memo also mentioned that the appellant cooperated with the police and the failure of the investigation did not relate to her testimony. As a result of the police memo, the appellant requested the respondent reconsider its position regarding her application. On 29 November 2007 the respondent informed D. that a review of her application and of the police documents did not find an ‘initial evidence’ [the lowest standard of proof in Israeli law] to determine that she was a victim of trafficking in persons. Consequently, the appellant requested a temporary injunction from the Court, which would prohibit her expulsion from Israel. On 15 January 2008 the Court made an order not to expel the appellant until another decision on the matter was given.

This case is related to a female victim who was transferred from Nizip, Turkey, to Istanbul and was kept at the residence of the defendants against her will. The defendants’ intention was to obtain a financial benefit by forcing the victim to work against her will.

In 1999, Defendant Maude Paulin, along with and her then-husband Saintfor Palin and her mother Evelyn Theodore, arranged to smuggle a then-fourteen-year-old girl from Haiti to the United States. According to evidence presented at trial, from 1999 to 2005, defendants used physical abuse and threats to force the victim to work as a domestic servant. The victim worked, without compensation, for approximately 15 hours each day, performing various household tasks such as cooking, cleaning, and yard work. Defendants further controlled and isolated the victim by threatening to have her arrested or deported to Haiti if she reported defendants to law enforcement. In June 2005, the victim escaped from the defendants with the assistance of a family friend who had witnessed this treatment.

Defendants Maude Paulin and Evelyn Theodore were found guilty by a federal jury of conspiring to violate the victim’s civil rights and of forcing the victim to work for them. The jury also found Maude Paulin and Saintfort Paulin guilty of harboring an illegal alien. A fourth defendant, C.T., was acquitted of the conspiracy and forced labor charges. Due to an illness, Theodore’s sentencing date has not yet been determined.

In February 2007, Rubén Darío Ardila Álvarez contacted two minors who lived in the municipality of Montenegro, Colombia, and offered them a job to work as maids and cooks in a hotel located in Cali, Colombia. The minors accepted the offer, but the day after they were taken to the municipality of Orito, Colombia, where they were confined to a bar called “Candilejas”. The two minors were told by Luis Armando Pérez Valencia that they had to work as prostitutes in order to pay back COP150,000 (USD85), the amount supposedly spent on transportation to Orito.

The traffickers threatened the victims and locked them in a room whenever they were not working. Six weeks later the minors managed to escape from Candilejas Bar and informed the authorities about what had happened. The police captured the defendants a few days later.

The defendants George and Adaobi Udeozor, husband and wife, smuggled a young girl from Nigeria to the United States to work for them as a domestic slave. In September 1996, George Udeozor traveled to Nigeria and falsely promised to the victim’s family that the Udeozors would adopt their daughter and provide her with a better education in the United States. The victim was 14 years old at the time. George Udeozor smuggled the victim into the United States using his oldest daughter’s passport. Once in the United States, the Udeozors forced the young girl to care for their children, prepare meals, and perform a number of other household tasks. The victim was also forced to work in Adaobi Udeozor’s medical office. The victim did not receive any compensation for her work, nor was she allowed to attend school. To maintain control over the victim, the defendants subjected her to physical, and emotional abuse. George Udeozor raped the victim on multiple occasions. The defendants also used the threat of arrest by immigration authorities as a means of controlling the victim. The victim was rescued in October 2001 after she managed to call the local police.

The appellant was accused of operating a widespread national organised crime network that engaged in the recruitment and transport of women for the purpose of engaging in commercial sexual exploitation (i.e. prostitution). A police sting operation netted a lower-level pimp and two prostitutes with connections to the appellant, and these individuals offered up confessions that, in conjunction with other circumstantial evidence, substantiated the charges against the appellant. It was disclosed that the appellant’s network supplied girls to five star hotels, guest houses and posh colony flats in various cities including Mumbai, Calcutta, Bangalore, etc., and that this prostitution racket had been ongoing since 1985-86.

In 2006, the defendant, who was approximately 28-years-old, picked up the 16-year-old female victim outside of a homeless shelter for juveniles in Greensboro, North Carolina. The defendant took her to his house, and allegedly coerced her to engage in commercial sex acts by locking her in a room until she agreed.

The defendant then drove the victim and several other adult females to Washington, D.C., where the defendant was a resident. He arranged for the victim's photo to be posted on Craigslist under the "erotic services" section, and on at least one occasion, made the victim "walk the track" in an area known for prostitution.

In June 2005, Mr M.T.S. and Ms R.R.C. were offered employment as chefs at the restaurants while still in the Philippines, as a result of a labour shortage in Canberra, ACT. They arrived in Australia on Business (Long Term) subclass 457 visas, sponsored by the restaurant owners. These owners were later prosecuted for several breaches of the Workplace Relations Act 1996 (Cth) during the employment of Mr M.T.S. and Ms R.R.C., mainly for failure to pay the appropriate award rate, as well as failure to pay overtime and penalty rates.

Mr M.T.S. had also complained about being underpaid and maltreated to the Department of Immigration and Multicultural Affairs (DIMIA), the union, and to the Philippines' embassy. He further alleged that, as a result of making these complaints, he was ‘kidnapped’ and almost forced to return to the Philippines against his will.

In the course of 2004, resorting to force, the accused had recruited, kept and kept in hiding two minor injured parties in his home, bringing clients with whom the injured parties had forced sexual intercourse with, taking the payment for this and when one of the injured parties tried to escape, he caught up with her and inflicting light bodily injuries, returned her to his home where he held her until the police appeared.

The victim was married but left her husband due to their strained relationship. She returned home to her parents but was not well received so she left for Tirana. On the way, she stopped at a restaurant and struck up a conversation with an individual. The person told her that he knew of someone in Durres who could help her find a job.

In Durres, she met up with the defendant and stayed at his home for a week. Then, the defendant told her that he would be travelling to visit his aunt, so they took a bus together to Vlora. In Vlora, the defendant met with several individuals, one of them being a man named Dhori. Dhori told the victim that he was bringing her to Italy to meet up with the defendant. Fredi Hoxha picked up the defendant and forced her into prostitution. A portion of the money was sent to the defendant in Albania. The defendant worked for three months but managed to escape with the help of an Italian client.

“Frosty Treats,” a Russian company operating ice-cream trucks near Kansas City, Missouri, promised a group of college students from the Ukraine the opportunity to earn salaries between $10,000 and $15,000 for the summer in the United States. Once in the United States, however, the students were forced to work 13 hours a day, seven days a week, for less than minimum wage. Defendants restricted the students' access to telephone and mail communication. On September 10, 2007, David Carslake pled guilty to obstruction of mail; Frosty Treats entered a separate settlement agreement, agreeing to pay more than $47,555 in restitution to the six students, and to stop recruiting foreign students at all of its U.S. locations for the next two years. Several of the other defendants remain at large.

On October 08, 1997, the defendant Luiz Arnaldo da Silva Martins, a taxi driver, promoted the output of the victims C.F.O., I.S.B. and J.R.C., who were minors at that time, for the purpose of sexual exploitation to an Argentine nightclub. With regard to the victims M.D. and A., the output was only in its attempted form, since the victims decided to call off the trip when they had already been inside of the defendant’s car. One month later, the victims C.F.O., I.S.B. and J.R.C. were deported from Argentina. The defendant Luiz Arnaldo da Silva Martins testified that he had taken the victims to Argentina, but he denied having known the purpose of the trip or the age of the victims.

This proceeding began with an investigation of the defendant Zhang Zhang for Forgery, Use of a Forged Instrument, Memorializing a False Statement, and Forgery of Seals and Sealed Documents. A search of this defendant’s home and statements made by this defendant produced evidence of further crimes including Human Trafficking and Trafficking in migrants, as well as evidence of the identities of several of Zhang Zhang’s co-conspirators. These co-conspirators included Zeballos Lizárraga, an advisor to the Ministry of Government (Ministerio de Gobierno), Yin Chen and Chavarria, who claimed to be the wives of Zhang Zhang and Zeballos Lizárraga, and three sitting politicians: National Supplementary Deputies del Rosio Seeghers and Leigue Hurtado and Constituent Assemblyman Bailaba Prapaino.

As the three politicians are the focus of the current case, it gives substantial detail only on the roles of these individuals in the underlying trafficking crimes. All three utilized their positions to solicit the entry of Chinese citizens into Bolivia for various purposes. This included personally writing letters to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to obtain the necessary visas. Specifically, the alleged illegal actions of the defendants are described as follows:

On 2006-10-10, PW 1, who is in-charge of NGO Prajwala lodged a written report at the police station, stating that the victim girl had lost her father in her childhood and was regularly beaten and tortured by her mother. She ran away from home and worked as a domestic servant in a house in Secunderabad city. After some time, she left that house also and reached Secunderabad railway station. At the station Accused no. 1 (hereinafter referred to as A1) approached her and promised to provide a good job and took her to Accused no. 2 (hereinafter referred to as A2), who then forced her into prostitution. One day she escaped from the clutches of the accused and managed to reach Prajwala.

After completion of investigation and filing of charge sheet the case was committed to the appropriate court. Charges were framed against A1 and A2 for the offences punishable under Section 366-A of IPC and Sections 3, 4 & 5 of ITP Act. A2 was also charged for the offence of rape under Section 376 of IPC. Both the accused pleaded not guilty for the said charges.

Based on the material on record and the arguments extended on either side the court framed the following points for determination.

1. Whether the testimony of the prosecutrix inspires total confidence in the court.

2. Whether the guilt of the accused for the offence punishable under Section 3 of the ITP Act is proved.

3. Whether the prosecution could prove the guilt of the accused for the offences punishable under Sections 4 & 5 of ITP Act.

4. Whether the guilt of A2 for the offence punishable under Section 376 of IPC is proved.

On the first point the court held that there were no relations between the accused and the prosecutrix earlier to the alleged episode of offences. Hence, it can not be alleged that she was prompted by any ulterior motives to speak against the accused; for which reason her testimony must be held to be true.

On the second point the court held that the evidence on record does not bring out evidence sufficient to fix the complicity of the accused in the offence punishable under Section 3 of ITP Act.

On the third point the court held Section 4 of ITP Act makes the act of any person over the age of 18 years living wholly or in part, on the earnings of prostitution of any person punishable. The evidence of PW 2 would amply prove that she was led into prostitution by A1 and A2. There can be no other reason that can be read into the facts of the case other than the monetary benefit. The charge under Section 5 of ITP Act was also proven against the accused.

The defence counsel sought to discredit the testimony of the victim, by stating that the prosecution was unable to prove that the victim had stayed in the house of A2. The court stated in its judgment that facts of the case would project a clear situation where no independent witnesses would come forward to give evidence. The failure of the police in not explaining about their efforts to secure independent witnesses cannot at any rate prejudice the victim. When the case itself stands on highly credible facts calling for independent evidence would result in a hyper technical approach, which is not warranted.

The defence counsel also sought to shatter the credibility of the NGO and PW 1. The court stated that the mere fact that the organisation of PW 1 is run by the funds which are provided to it based on the number of victims catered by it can not be taken to infer that every act of it is motivated by the said benefit. Hence the suggestion that PW 1 has shown PW 2 as a member of their rescue home in order to raise funds is simply ridiculous.

On the fourth point the court held that the evidence of the victim clearly shows that A2 apart from using her as a tool for prostitution had also used her as a tool to satisfy his own lust. The testimony of the victim as true was held in the first point itself. Hence, charge of A2 raping the victim had been proved.

Having found the accused guilty on several counts, the court sentenced A1 and A2 as described below.

The defendants – two Polish women – contacted several Polish women from poor families living in the countryside and offered to find them jobs as babysitters or cleaners in London. The three victims who went to London were forced to work as prostitutes. One of these victims escaped with the help of her compatriots. Money obtained by the women exploited as prostitutes was received directly by the daughters of the defendants but the defendants participated in the profits. None of the three courts deciding the case had any doubt that the crime of which the defendants were accused constituted trafficking in persons. Six out of the eight victims participated in the court proceedings and gave witness testimony.

Before the trial, E.L. did not admit to committing the crimes; she claimed to have no knowledge of the fact that the women were brought from Poland to London for prostitution. E.L. alleged that she tried to help the women in good faith as they were having serious financial problems and most of them were unemployed and abused alcohol. E.L. denied luring the victims to go to London and forcing any of them to become prostitutes. After having pleaded guilty at the first hearing, E.L. pleaded not guilty.

The court found that E.L.’s statements were not convincing and that she was fully aware of the criminal nature of the practices she was engaged with together with the other defendant – A.M. – and her two daughters, who lived in London. The court analyzed the evidence, mainly witness testimony, in detail. The court found that the defendant was aware of having committed the crimes and suffered from no mental disorder despite the fact that she was hospitalized three times in a mental clinic.

A.M. did not admit to committing the crimes; she explained that she was not aware of the fact that her daughters were engaged in luring women abroad for prostitution and benefited from the prostitution of others. A.M. alleged that her daughters worked in London as babysitters and cleaners, and the woman she saw at their apartment were temporary occupants. A.M. stated that she looked for women who could work in London as babysitters or cleaners at the request of her daughter; she tried to help the women because they were unemployed and were in difficult economic circumstances. A.M. pleaded not guilty.

The court found that A.M.’s statements were not convincing and that she had attempted to lure both victims to London to become prostitutes. The court analyzed the testimonies given by the victims and other witnesses and found no exonerating evidence. The court concluded that A.M. was fully aware of the nature of practices in which her daughters were engaged in London and looked for good-looking young women who would be willing to travel to London for work. She was financially supported by her daughters who took benefit from the prostitution of others; therefore, she benefitted from these practices indirectly. A.M. also threatened to instigate criminal proceedings against the sons of a woman who had become aware of the trafficking practices, which was also confirmed by telephone call records. The court concluded that the defendant was aware of her actions at the time of the crimes and suffered from no mental disorder despite the fact that she was treated for depression for several years and had occasional epileptic seizures.

The courts found that both defendants committed trafficking in persons (including in the form of attempt).

Between June 1, 1999, and June 21, 2004, Zavala and Ibanez orchestrated a scheme to illegally obtain visas for Peruvian aliens seeking to come into the United States. The Civil Rights Division led a long and difficult investigation resulting in a 22-count indictment against five defendants charged with subjecting workers to involuntary servitude in a garment factory in American Samoa. The victims, some of whom were held for up to two years, were forced to work through extreme food deprivation, beatings, and physical restraint. The victims were held in barracks on a guarded company compound, and were threatened with confiscation of their passports, deportation, economic bankruptcy, severe economic hardship to family members, false arrest, and a host of other consequences. Frequently the victims were forced to catch and eat dogs because their food stores had not been replenished.

Ms DS was an employee of brothel owner Ms Wei Tang who has been convicted for offences relating to sexual slavery: R v Wei Tang (2008) 238 CLR 1. The initials DS are used to identify the accused due to a suppression order placed on her name, after she gave evidence against her employer.

Ms Tang was accused, and later convicted, of having purchased five women from Thailand to work in debt-bondage conditions in a legal brothel called ‘Club 417’ in Fitzroy. The women had previously worked in the sex industry in Thailand and were aware that they would be working in brothels in Australia. They arrived in Australia separately between August 2002 and May 2003 on validly obtained tourist visas, although it was not disclosed in the visa application that the true purpose was to work. It is unclear how much of the visa application process was understood by the victims: R v Wei Tang (2007) 16 VR 454, [5]. On the flight from Bangkok to Sydney the victim would usually be ‘escorted’ by an elderly couple, so as to avoid suspicion. On arrival in Australia a representative of an Australian ‘owner’ would meet the victim and ‘escorts’. The representative would pay off the ‘escorts’ and transport the victim to a hotel where she was kept until a decision was made as to which brothel she was to work at.

Ms Tang owned the licensed brothel ‘Club 417’ and held a 70 per cent interest in a syndicate which bought four of the five women with the remaining 30 per cent held by Ms DS who negotiated with recruiters in Thailand, and her associates. Other ‘owners’ brought the fifth woman to Australia. This fifth person worked in another brothel and was subsequently moved to ‘Club 417’.Ms DS was herself a previous victim of Ms Wei Tang and had chosen to stay with her trafficker after she had repaid her contract debt. She had previously worked under similar circumstances in the sex industry in Hong Kong. Ms DS, a Thai national, was responsible for supervision of the contract workers at ‘Club 417’, the brothel owned by Ms Wei Tang. She also moved money between Wei Tang and an organiser in Sydney, known as Sam: R v DS (2005) 153 A Crim R 194, [7].

When the women testified against Ms Tang, they explained that they had voluntarily entered into agreements with a broker in Thailand, and owed between AU$ 40,000 and 45,000 to the owner of these ‘contracts’. Ms Tang had purchased these contracts from the Thai recruiter for AU$ 20,000. Repayments of this AUD 20,000 formed the basis for the charges of slavery that were brought against Ms Tang and her employee, Ms DS.

The debt owed to Ms Tang had to be repaid by the victims by working in a brothel six days a week over a period of four to six months. This required serving up to 900 clients. Customers at ‘Club 417’ were charged AU$ 110.00. Ms Tang retained AU$ 43.00 in her capacity as brothel owner plus 70 per cent of the remaining AU$ 67.00 for four of the women and Ms DS and her associates received 30 per cent. In relation to the fifth woman, after Ms Tang took her AU$ 43.00 fee, the other AU$ 67.00 was divided between her owners. The victims were offered to work on their free day and keep the AU$ 50.00 otherwise used to pay the debt.

Whilst the women were not usually under ‘lock and key’ there were a number of factors that served to prevent them from escaping; they had little money and limited English, their passports were retained, their visas had been obtained illegally, they feared detection by immigration authorities, and they worked long hours: R v Tang (2008) 238 CLR 1, [15]–[18]. There was no other evidence of physical maltreatment by the accused. It was conceded that two of the five women had indeed repaid their debts, had their passports returned and had voluntarily stayed on to work as paid sex workers.

Ms DS pleaded guilty to two counts of slave trading (s 270.3(1)(b) Criminal Code (Cth)) and three counts of possessing a slave (s 270.3(1)(a)). The conviction for possession of a slave was in respect of Ms DS’s work in escorting and supervising three contract workers, whereas the conviction for slave trading was based on her taking possession of the women once they arrived in Australia: R v DS (2005) 153 A Crim R 194, [8]–[10].

The Defendant, through a recruiting agent in India (“Mithun”) and a consultant in Malaysia (“Singh”), hired a group of Indian nationals between the ages of 21 and 35 to work as general labourers. Fifty-two of the men eventually hired by the Defendant and flown to Malaysia under this recruiting scheme, the Plaintiffs, brought a suit against the Defendant, alleging breach of the terms of employment they were offered prior to their departure from India.

In order to protect its citizens from unfair practices in such situations, the Indian government required various documents and minimum terms of employment to be provided by potential employers. These documents include (i) a demand letter stating the terms of employment that the potential employer is offering, (ii) a contract of employment to be signed by the employer and each employee, (iii) a power of attorney authorising the recruiter to act on behalf of the employer in this regard, and (iv) an affidavit from the employer undertaking to repatriate the employees at its expense and to return passports to the employees. The Defendant, through Mithun and Singh, provided such documents to the authorities and the Plaintiffs were allowed to depart for Malaysia.

Three employees gave testimony on behalf of the Plaintiffs. While each of the three stated that they were offered slightly different terms of employment, each of the employees stated that, upon arriving in Malaysia, they were informed that the actual pay and benefits being offered by the Defendant were substantially lower than they were informed of while in India. In order to secure the job, each plaintiff had raised 100,000 Indian Rupies to cover the costs of (they were told) levies, medical check-ups, visas and airfare. Prior to departing India Mithun collected all but roughly USD1000 from the Plaintiffs. But upon arrival in Malaysia Singh collected the remainder of the funds.

When they complained about their wages, other migrant workers instructed them to visit the Indian High Commission to obtain a copy of their contracts. A group of the employees visited the High Commission but discovered that the contracts on file had been signed by the Managing Director of the Company, but not the individual employees. Further, upon returning to work the employees found that their time cards were missing and were informed that if they wished to return to work they would need to sign new contracts in line with the lower wage offered by the Defendant.

The Plaintiffs continued to complain about the situation and were subsequently informed that the employer would be sending them all back to India. Several of the employees locked themselves in the hostel out of protest, leading the Defendant to shut off the water and electricity.

On the stand Singh admitted that two sets of documents were sent to India. One set offered the real terms of employment that the Plaintiffs were informed of after arriving in Malaysia. The second set of documents, upon which the Plaintiffs were relying, were prepared merely to satisfy the Indian government’s requirements in terms of minimum wages and conditions.

The 1st instance Judge convicted the defendants to the minimum imprisonment for the crime, 5 years of imprisonment that would initially begin in a semi-open prison regime, for committing the crime foreseen in article 231, caput, of the Penal Code – international trafficking of people for sexual exploitation.

The defendant’s appealed from the 1st Instance decision and attempted to prove that they were not involved in the recruitment, deceiving and international trafficking of people for sexual exploitation. The defendant’s declared that they believed that the victims were going to Spain to work as waitresses, and that the entire criminal scheme was operationalized by Antonio Martinez, a Spanish national that worked with the Varig group, and simply asked Paulo Silva to hand the victims two envelopes.

The 2nd Instance Judge verified that the evidence in the legal process effectively proves the involvement of the 3 defendants in the international trafficking of the victims for sexual exploitation in Spain. The 1st Instance conviction was amended because the minimum time of imprisonment for the crime foreseen in article 231, caput, of the Penal Code is 3 years in an initially semi-open prison regime. As such, the defendant’s time of imprisonment was reduced to 3 years in a semi-open prison regime. The remaining 1st Instance verdict was upheld.

The petitioner, an Advocate, filed a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) before the Supreme Court (SC) of India, based on an article "A Red Light Trap: Society gives no chance to prostitutes' offspring" published in the magazine 'India Today' dated July 11, 1988. The petitioner prayed for establishing separate educational institutions for the children of the fallen women (term used by the SC throughout the judgment). The SC stated in its order dated 15-11-1989 that “segregating children of prostitutes by locating separate schools and providing separate hostels would not be in the interest of the children and the society at large”. While the SC did not accept the plea for separate hostels for children of prostitutes, it felt that "accommodation in hostels and other reformatory homes should be adequately available to help segregation of these children from their mothers living in prostitute homes as soon as they are identified".

The SC constituted a Committee directing it to submit a report giving suggestions for appropriate action. Upon submission of the report of the Committee, the SC formulated the following questions for decision: -

- What are the rights of the children of fallen women, the modules to segregate them from their mothers and others so as to give them protection, care and rehabilitation in the mainstream of the national life?

- What should be the scheme to be evolved to eradicate prostitution, i.e., the source itself; and what succour and sustenance can be provided to the fallen victims of flesh trade?

In its judgment, the SC quoted the Fundamental Rights of women and children from the Constitution of India (namely, Articles 14, 15, 16, 21, 23, 24, 38, 39, 45, 46) and relevant international instruments. The court deliberated on the reasons for prostitution and the continuation of the victims in profession and recognized that the victims are the poor, illiterate and ignorant sections of the society who are the target group in the flesh trade; rich communities exploit them and harvest at their misery and ignominy in an organised gangsterism, in particular, with police nexus. The court held that women found in the flesh trade, should be viewed more as victims of adverse socio-economic circumstances rather than as offenders in our society. Equally, the right of the child is the concern of the society so that fallen women surpass trafficking of her person from exploitation; contribute to bring up her children; live a life with dignity; and not to continue in the foul social environment. Equally, the children have the right to equality of opportunity, dignity and care, protection and rehabilitation by the society with both hands open to bring them into the mainstream of social life without pre-stigma affixed on them for no fault of her/his.

The SC stated that three Cs, viz., Counselling, Cajoling and Coercion were necessary to effectively enforce the provisions of various statutes. The role of NGOs in rehabilitating and educating the children of the fallen women was emphasized. Detailed directions were given for rescue, rehabilitation of prostitutes and children of prostitutes. The SC held that society was responsible for a woman becoming a victim of circumstances therefore, society should make reparation to prevent trafficking in women, rescue them from red light areas and other areas in which the women were driven or trapped in prostitution. Their rehabilitation by socio-economic empowerment and justice, is the constitutional duty of the State. Their economic empowerment and social justice with dignity of person, are the fundamental rights and the Court and the Government should positively endeavour to ensure them.

A citizen informed the police authorities about the existence of an agency that posted newspaper ads offering young women the opportunity to work as dancers in Japan. She claimed that her daughters, M. and L., had responded to the ad and that it had aroused her suspicions. The Seccional de Policía Judicial e Investigación (Local Branch of the Judicial and Investigative Police, Colombia) organized an operation to send a police officer from their agency, posing as a dancer interested in the activities offered. The officer discovered that the agency would provide money to applicants to obtain a passport, that they took photos of the applicants in traditional costumes and that they were not interested in prior dancing experience. Applicants were also shown pornographic magazines. The employment contract required a USD5,000 bill of exchange, guaranteed by a guarantor in case the applicant were to violate the agreement.

Three of the traffickers—Erdenedali, Erdenemonkh, and Purevdoj—met a Chinese citizen at a border town who apparently encouraged them bring Mongolian women to the town of Er-Lian, where he would arrange for them to engage in sexual transactions in China. Erdenemonkh and Purevdoj recruited two women working in prostitution in Ulaanbaatar, and Erdenedalai secured financing from Tsendgombo.

The three men brought the two women to Er-Lian, where their sexual services were sold to five or six clients per day. The men kept 40% of the money earned, threatened to break the womens’ legs if they ran away, and discussed the possibility of selling their kidneys. Erdenedalai then sold the women in China, but kept their passports. Soon after, the women escaped to the Mongolian consulate. After the women filed a report, the men were arrested and confessed to recruiting women for prostitution, selling them for a profit in China, and leaving them without passports.

Despite evidence that the women were held under coercive conditions, they were fined for agreeing to engage in prostitution in China.

The defendant recruited the women by placing an advertisement in a newspaper seeking women dancers to travel to Yugoslavia and Romania for USD 3,000 per month. The idea allegedly came from Maxim’s sister Marina, who was living in Yugoslavia. The women travelled with Maxim to Beijing where he arranged for their visas. Upon arriving in Yugoslavia, the women were forced into sexual servitude by Marina and Maxim, and were denied food and forced into household work if they refused. They were also raped by Maxim. The women were sold to a Yugoslavian mafia member in 2001. They were eventually able to call their families in Mongolia, and were discovered in a police raid.

The women pressed charges when they returned to Mongolia, and Maxim was arrested when he returned to Mongolia to recruit additional women. Marina was unable to be located in Mongolia and was not arrested or charged.

After meeting Mr Lennox at a downtown Montreal nightclub, the victim, a 17-year-old girl, was seduced and later brought to Toronto. Mr Lennox eventually forced her into prostitution and took control of all her earnings. As the victim initially did not have the necessary identification documents for employment in an exotic dance club, she was made to prostitute on the street, and then as an escort and exotic dancer. The victim was also subjected to threats and intimidation when she wished to leave the sex trade.

The defendant met a person named Yehia who coerced him to sell his kidney for 1500 dollars. The defendant traveled to Iraq with Yehia, who confiscated the defendant’s passport upon arrival, gave it to a man named Talal, and received 500 dollars in return. Talal then took the defendant to Al-Khayyal Hospital in Baghdad and performed a surgery to remove his left kidney. Once the defendant returned to Jordan, he found 500 dollars in his bank account.

Later, Yehia met with the defendant and asked him to accompany two men to Iraq to sell their kidneys. The defendant accompanied the two men to Iraq, took them to Talal, and received 300 dollars in return. While the defendant was in Iraq, the 300 dollars was stolen. The defendant was forced to return to Jordan without money and had to leave his passport in Iraq. At a later date, the defendant falsely notified the Security Center that his passport was lost. As a result, he was referred to the Anti-Corruption Directorate and was prosecuted.

The acts he committed, including selling his kidney and convincing three persons to sell their kidneys for 1300 dollars, are prohibited in Articles 10 and 4/c of the Jordanian Law on the Utilization of Human Organs. In addition, leaving his passport with the driver is prohibited under Article 18/b of the Passports Law.

The Court sentenced the defendant to one year in prison for each act committed offences under Articles 10 and 4/c of the Law on the Utilization of Human Organs. The defendant was also sentenced to 6 months in prison for violating Article 18/b of the Passports Law.

The defendant coerced another person to sell his kidney for 3500 dollars in Egypt through a third party. The victim travelled to Cairo in 2007, had his kidney removed at a hospital and received 500 dollars. The victim returned to Jordan where he was arrested for selling an organ for profit.

The Court sentenced the defendant to four months in prison for his involvement in promoting the selling of organs for profit which is prohibited under Article (80/1) of the Jordanian Penal Code and Articles 5 and 10 of the Law on the Utilization of Human Organs. Due to the defendant’s young age, the sentence was commuted to one month in prison based upon Article 72 of the Penal Code.

The Public Prosecutor’s complaint jointly with the Federal Police report, illustrate that the defendant recruited a victim for sexual exploitation sometime in 1999 through fraudulent means.

Moreover, the victim’s testimony, submitted through a letter rogatory, conveys that the defendant owned a brothel in Uruguaiana and that he has been in her neighbourhood looking for women to provide domestic cleaning services. The neighbours had recommended her as a potential employee. After the victim accepted this job offer to provide domestic cleaning services, the defendant took care of all the border crossing requirements to Brazil. When the victim arrived at the defendant’s house, she provided domestic cleaning services during the day and, in the evenings, was offered the opportunity to work as a prostitute, which the victim immediately refused to do. Upon noticing the victim’s situation, a man contacted the Federal Police and helped the victim quit working for the defendant.

Another witness, C.A.T., testified that he and the Federal Police headed to the defendant’s house to search and seize the victim. Upon their arrival, they found four girls. None were under 18 years of age and one of them was Argentinean. None of the girls claimed they were working as prostitutes. Instead, they claimed to be forcefully imprisoned. Though, when giving their report at a later time, the four girls claimed that they were only spending a month at the defendant’s house and could return to their home at any time they desired.

The main defendant N.N., with the aim of creating a network of brothels, organized a criminal group consisting of six other persons.

The group sought girls in Samara and Ulyanovsk provinces, as well as in the Republic of Chuvashia, in order to engage them in prostitution. To this end, they met women, offered them car rides and took them to N. N. in Tolyatti.

Furthermore, the perpetrators placed advertisements in regional newspapers for the recruitment of waitresses to work in a café. Threatening violence, they forced the women responding to the advertisements to work as prostitutes.

In the cities of Tolyatti, Ulyanovsk and Samara, N. N. organized a total of three brothels, which contained no fewer than 27 girls, including two minors.

The apartments in which the women were held were guarded. Those who managed to escape were found, beaten and brought back by the criminals. One of the women jumped out of a window and was taken to hospital with leg and hand fractures.

In 2006 in Pyatigorsk, O. M. organized illegal activities for the provision of paid sexual services. To that end, she engaged nine accomplices. In accordance with the plan, each member of the association strictly carried out the functions ascribed to them and received a share of the illicit profits. The structure of the criminal association included two functionally separate groups. The first group was responsible for selecting women for prostitution and their recruitment, transportation and transfer for the purpose of sexual exploitation. The second group was responsible for the organization of sexual services.

With the aim of preventing the women from refusing to participate in prostitution, as well as stopping their subsequent contact with law enforcement agencies, members of the criminal association made death threats and in a number of cases used physical force. As a result of the criminal activities of this association, 13 young women, of whom 4 were minors, were involved in prostitution.

The traffickers befriended the victims and lured them through Facebook and other social media sites to a private residence. The youngest victim believed she would be attending the residence for a friendly sleepover. The victims were drugged, forced to dress in minimal clothing, obliged to pose for pornographic photos, and required to lie about their age to clients. As added control, the traffickers confiscated the victims’ personal belongings and used violence and threats to ensure compliance. The traffickers set up the dates and arranged travel for the victims to meet their clients for sexual purposes in exchange for money. The traffickers collected the money resulting from the victims’ sexual services.

The accused detained an 18 years old girl for prostitution and forced her to have an abortion. The girls come from different provinces and they work in a brothel for a salary of 3000 baht. The accused claimed not to have known that the girls were under 18 years old.

She stayed with them for two days, after which they took her to another house where they brought Pakistani, Indian, and Bangladeshi nationals to engage in sexual intercourse with her for money. Defendant 2 confessed that they had contacted the victim when they were in Pakistan, offered to procure her an Omani work visa in 2009, met the victim at Muscat International Airport and then took her to their house in Suhar where she stayed with them for two days. They later rented a house for her where she was used for prostitution.

Defendant 1 encouraged Defendant 2 to escape from her sponsor to engage in prostitution for financial gain.

Defendant 1 sold Defendant 2 to Defendant 3 for 100 Omani Rials. According to the documented confessions of Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, Defendant 3 engaged in sexual intercourse with Defendant 2 and brought in other individuals to do likewise in exchange for money.

The investigation unit of Nizwa Police received a report from a reliable source regarding the involvement of three Asian women in prostitution in Nizwa Province in an apartment that was rented to a company specializing in selling natural herbs. After verifying the information, the Public Prosecution issued a warrant to search the apartment. The investigation team arrived at the scene and arrested three women who were caught “in flagrante delicto.”

Interrogation revealed that the women were victims of an organized criminal group, which had deliberately engaged in the crime of human trafficking and committed all forms of sexual exploitation. The group also provided transportation and accommodations for the three victims by both legal and illegal means using coercion, intimidation and deception—taking advantage of their difficult living conditions to profit financially.

The defendants brought two girls (age 14 and age 17), to the United States from Cameroon, in the mid-1990s. The defendants told the girls and their families that, in exchange for performing light housework, the girls would have the opportunity to attend school in the United States. Once in the United States, the defendants used threats and physical violence, including sexual abuse, to force the victims to work long days as domestic servants and nannies. The defendants also controlled and manipulated the girls by threatening to deport them. The victims received no compensation, and were not permitted to attend school.

The defendant has promoted the victim’s travel from Brazil to Europe (initially to Germany, then to Switzerland), the place where the victim was sexually explored as a prostitute and was kept in a false imprisonment.

The defendant obliged the victim to charge 200 Francos of each of client and to present a minimum daily income 1.000 Francos.

During the investigations was found that the modus operandi used by the defendant to bring girls to Europe for prostitution was: initially he simulated the advent of a feeling between him and the victim, after he had won their trust, he offered them "work" in Europe providing yet passports and payment of all relevant expenses; once arrived in Europe, he forced them into prostitution.

An official document n. 87/88 issued by the German Embassy in Brasilia, indicates the involvement of the accused in several other previous offenses, including prostitution, and even condemnation in Germany.

For Judge of the case was sufficiently proven that the defendant promoted the exit of the victim J.D.P.A. of Brazil to Europe (primarily Germany, then to Switzerland), where there was exploitation of the prostitution.

In January 2003, the defendant, Kelvin Scott, prostituted a 13-year-old female runaway, “S.H.”, in Amarillo, Texas, and Oklahoma City, Oklahoma. The defendant and a female prostitute lured the victim from an Oklahoma City bus stop by inviting S.H. to a party, and by offering her drugs and alcohol. The defendant also promised her nice clothes and “money in her pocket.” S.H. was instructed that she must return each night with $500 to $1,000, all to be given to the defendant. The defendant previously employed five individuals, including another minor, as prostitutes.

Dennis Warren provided migrant farm workers for the farm of Cecil Williams in Nash County, North Carolina, during the summer of 1981, and also supervised the workers. Dennis assisted in running the crew with his brother, Richard Warren, John Harris, and Halsey Norwood. Many of the workers were recruited by methods ranging from deception to kidnapping. The workers were charged for their consumption in the camp where they lived, and the costs were deducted from their wages. The workers were guarded at night, and anyone who tried to flee would be picked up and returned by Harris or others. Both physical and threatened violence were used to prevent workers from leaving, and to force them to work faster. Workers who complained of illness or injuries were denied medical assistance.

On September 13, 1981, R.A., a migrant worker from Philadelphia, died on a bus he had been placed in after collapsing in the fields. Two autopsies established that the primary cause of death was heat stroke. His death and reports of civil rights violations at the farm precipitated an investigation of the camp by the FBI.

In 2005, the defendant began smuggling Latin American women into the United States from Costa Rica, Columbia, and Guatemala for between $15,000-$20,000 per woman. Once in the United States, Monsalve forced the women to work as prostitutes to pay off their smuggling fees.

Most women knew they would work as prostitutes and were expected to work between 6 and 7 days per week, and have sex with between 20 and 25 men per night. The women charged $30 for 15 minutes of sex, with defendant keeping $15 and applying the other $15 to the debt. After the debt was repaid, the women could continue working for defendant as prostitutes under the same profit sharing agreement.

However, at least two victims were promised legitimate work. In one instance, victims 1 and 2 refused to engage in prostitution and were threatened with deportation if they went to the police.
